verdict: Warrants a native audition after direct source-versus-runtime comparison. The conspicuous source holes that rejected v1 are not visible in these v2 images.
confirmedImprovements: Both sacks retain continuous cloth volumes with rounded folds and pinched seams; the repeated sharp black triangular punctures of v1 are absent in these views.
The jug body, moulded handle and neck form a coherent continuous object from both sides. Its underside contact and handle recess still need an oblique native check.

Individual cans have curved shells, rims and readable openings. Cardboard corrugation, torn edges, fabric drape and separate stone volumes resolve real construction that the original faceted mound lacked.
The overall pile silhouette closely follows the supplied reference while retaining recognizable separate objects. These improvements are visible regardless of the reported polygon count.
remainingConcerns: Materials are pale and broadly similar under this source lighting. Compared with the reference, sack weave and stains, jug abrasion, oxidized can metal and the separation of cardboard from cloth are subdued. Check the complete PBR maps in native sun and shade before deciding whether this is source lighting or insufficient material contrast.

The tall sack has broad soft regions, and the fabric and cardboard meet in a few ambiguous joins. Verify nearby oblique views so local fusing or inflated reconstruction is not hidden by the two review angles.

The thin base of cloth and cardboard continues around much of the pile. Its perimeter must be embedded naturally into actual paving or soil; it must not float as a separate flat island or cast a uniform raised outline.

Runtime reduction must preserve can rims and wall thickness, the jug handle opening, separated cardboard flutes, sack seam folds and small stone silhouettes. Increasing or reducing counts alone cannot establish that.
